label: Yesha'yahu (Isaiah) — 1QIsa-a — Part 2 — Chapters 13–27
summary_plain: Yesha'yahu delivers oracles against the nations. The burden against Babylon — YHWH musters the host for battle. The burden against Moav. The burden against Dameshek. The burden against Cush — the land shadowing with wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia sends ambassadors by sea. The burden against Mitsrayim. The burden against the desert of the sea. The burden against Tsor. Yesha'yahu's apocalypse: YHWH will punish the host of heaven on high and the kings of the earth. On this mountain he will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and the Orit Ge'ez. The oracle cycle (chapters 13-23) positions YHWH as sovereign over all nations — not a tribal deity but the judge of the entire earth. Yesha'yahu 18 is critical: the 'land shadowing with wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia' that sends ambassadors by sea to 'a nation scattered and peeled' is a geographic description with no parallel in the ancient Near Eastern prophetic corpus. The apocalyptic section (chapters 24-27) describes universal judgment and the swallowing of death — language the Qumran community read as eschatological but not as a divine incarnation event.

key_terms.definition: A series of judgment pronouncements in Yesha'yahu 13-23 against Babylon, Assyria, Plishtim, Moav, Damascus, Mitzrayim, and others; YHWH's sovereignty extends over all peoples.
A theme running through Yesha'yahu's oracles: a day when YHWH intervenes decisively to judge the proud and exalt the lowly; Babylon's fall is a paradigm of this day.
Chapters 24-27 of Yesha'yahu — a cosmic vision of the earth laid waste, kings imprisoned, death swallowed, and the dead rising; among the earliest resurrection texts in the Hebrew corpus.
Yesha'yahu 25:8 declares that YHWH will swallow up death forever and wipe tears from all faces; this ancient Hebrew text is the source the NT borrowed its resurrection language from.
Yesha'yahu 26:19 — 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise'; one of the earliest explicit statements of bodily resurrection in the pre-Rabbinic corpus.
Yesha'yahu 14:12 addresses the king of Babylon: 'How you have fallen from heaven, O shining one, son of the dawn!' — a taunt over a human tyrant's pride and fall, not a cosmic being.
Yesha'yahu 25:6-10 describes YHWH hosting a feast on Mount Tziyon for all peoples; the nations stream to Yerushalayim to receive YHWH's salvation.
Yesha'yahu 22 describes the Valley of Vision — a lament over Yerushalayim's leaders who celebrate while the city faces destruction; Shevna the steward is condemned.
Yesha'yahu 19 pronounces judgment on Mitzrayim — the Nile dries up, its wisdom fails — but ends with Mitzrayim, Assyria, and Yisra'el as a threefold blessing in the earth.
Yesha'yahu 13-14 pronounces Babylon's downfall on the Day of YHWH; the great city will become like Sodom and Amora — never inhabited again.

faq.question: What is the 'Yesha'yahu Apocalypse' in chapters 24-27?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 24-27 is a cosmic vision unlike anything in the surrounding chapters. The earth is emptied and twisted, the heavenly host imprisoned, kings judged, and death itself swallowed. Chapter 26:19 contains one of the earliest resurrection texts in Hebrew scripture. These chapters share imagery with the Enochic tradition and the DSS, confirming pre-Corruption Hebrew roots.

faq.question: Is the 'shining one, son of the dawn' in Yesha'yahu 14 a cosmic being?
faq.answer: No. Yesha'yahu 14:12 is explicitly a taunt-song over the king of Babylon (14:4). The shining star language is a poetic exaggeration of the tyrant's pride: he thought himself exalted to heaven, but he has fallen to Sheol. This is a human ruler mocked after his downfall, not a cosmic adversary. Later Rabbinic and Christian traditions imposed a cosmic reading that the text does not support.

faq.question: What does Yesha'yahu 25:8 teach about death?
faq.answer: YHWH will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from every face. This ancient Hebrew declaration is the source for all later resurrection hope. The NT borrowed its language from this text; the direction of borrowing is ancient-to-later, not the reverse.

faq.question: Why is Yesha'yahu 19's ending about Mitzrayim unexpected?
faq.answer: After pronouncing severe judgment on Mitzrayim (the Nile drying, wisdom failing, the people turning to idols), Yesha'yahu 19 ends with a remarkable promise: Mitzrayim will know YHWH, build an altar to him, and together with Assyria and Yisra'el become a triple blessing in the earth (19:24-25). This affirms YHWH's sovereignty over all nations, including traditional enemies.

faq.question: What is the 'everlasting covenant' broken in Yesha'yahu 24:5?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 24:5 says the earth is defiled because its inhabitants broke the everlasting covenant. The DSS community understood this as the covenant given at Sinai and before, embedded in creation order. Breaking it defiles the land itself, not just individual people — a covenant accountability spanning all humanity, not only Yisra'el.

faq.question: What is the Day of YHWH in Yesha'yahu 13?
faq.answer: The Day of YHWH in Yesha'yahu 13:6-13 is described as a day of wrath when YHWH destroys sinners from the earth. It comes 'as destruction from the Almighty.' The stars and sun and moon are darkened; the heavens are shaken. Babylon is the immediate target, but the Day is cosmic in scope.

faq.question: How does Yesha'yahu 26:19 relate to the DSS resurrection texts?
faq.answer: Yesha'yahu 26:19 — 'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise' — is among the Hebrew corpus's earliest explicit bodily resurrection statements. The DSS community at Qumran preserved and cited this tradition, and the Enochic corpus develops the same theme. These are all pre-Rabbinic, pre-Christian texts; the resurrection tradition originates in this ancient Hebrew stream.

faq.question: What judgment does Yesha'yahu 24:21 announce for the heavenly host?
faq.answer: YHWH will punish 'the host of heaven in heaven' as well as earthly kings. They will be gathered as prisoners in a pit and shut up in a prison for many days. This is a parallel to the Enochic tradition of the Watchers imprisoned in an abyss — both texts draw on the same pre-Corruption Hebrew theology of cosmic judgment.

faq.question: What is the significance of the threefold holiness cry in context of Yesha'yahu 6?
faq.answer: The seraphim's cry in Yesha'yahu 6:3 — 'Holy, holy, holy is YHWH of Hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory' — is the acclamation of YHWH's cosmic kingship. It contrasts with the human King Uzziyahu who died (6:1): YHWH's throne endures. The threefold repetition is an intensifier in Hebrew idiom expressing the absolute completeness of YHWH's holiness.

faq.question: What nations are covered in the oracles of Yesha'yahu 13-23?
faq.answer: The oracles cover Babylon (13-14), Assyria (14:24-27), Plishtim (14:28-32), Moav (15-16), Damascus and Efrayim (17), Kush (18), Mitzrayim (19-20), Edom and Arabia (21), Tyre (23), and the Valley of Vision (Yerushalayim, 22). YHWH's judgment extends over every political power of the ancient world.
